documents.subject: The Washington Post's per-comparator salary/compensation explanations (Justin Gillis, Peter Goodman, Michael Fromson, Matthew Segal, Timothy Smart, Daniel Southerland) relative to Martha Hamilton and Marcia Mayer

pages.transcript:
CONFIDENTIAL INFORMATION UNDER THE AGREED ARBITRATION PROCEDURES
PREPARED FOR SETTLEMENT PURPOSES

Gillis received a high salary when he joined The Post as a reporter in Metro. His starting salary at The Post was more than the salaries of Hamilton or Mayer at that time.

Gillis is considered a standout reporter and a brilliant writer who does important work in the area of biotechnology. He is one of the pre-eminent biotechnology reporters in the country, which makes him a valued reporter in the marketplace.

Peter Goodman

Peter Goodman was paid substantially more than Hamilton on the 2000 to 2002 salary snapshots.

Goodman was paid more than Mayer and Skrzycki on the 2000 salary snapshot and substantially more than Mayer and Skrzycki on the 2001 and 2002 salary snapshots.

Experience and Education
Goodman came to The Post in the late 1990s as a reporter in the Metro/Anne Arundel Bureau. He became a reporter in Financial News in 1999, later becoming the reporter in Asia for Financial News. Prior to starting at The Post, Goodman worked as a reporter for the Anchorage Daily News for almost three years. He also worked for five months as a reporter for the Sacramento Bee and seven months as a regional correspondent for the Japan Times. Goodman is a graduate of Reed College and has a Masters in Asian Studies from the University of California at Berkeley.

Starting Salary
Upon starting at The Post, Goodman received approximately a 62 percent increase over his prior salary as a reporter at the Anchorage Daily News. His starting salary was substantially less than the salaries of Hamilton, Mayer and Skrzycki at that time.

Salary History
As of September 1, 2002, Goodman received seven merit increases - five of which he received as a reporter in Financial News. He received these five merit increases in the following years: 1999, 2000, 2001 and 2002. In 2000, Goodman received a substantial salary increase - roughly 40 percent - in response to a competing offer from The Wall Street Journal.

Explanation:
Goodman is considered one of the best reporters in Financial News, covering a difficult topic - telecommunications - that The Post considers important. He was given approximately a 40 percent salary increase during his first year covering

CONFIDENTIAL INFORMATION UNDER THE AGREED ARBITRATION PROCEDURES
PREPARED FOR SETTLEMENT PURPOSES

Upon starting at The Post, Fromson received approximately a 16 percent increase over his prior salary at Fortune Magazine. His starting salary was slightly more than the salary of Hamilton at that time and more than the salary of Mayer at that time.

Salary History
Fromson received one merit increase during his time at The Post. He received that merit increase as a reporter in Financial News in 1994.

Explanation:
The differential between the salary of Fromson and the salaries of Hamilton and Mayer is due to Fromson's high starting salary, which reflects The Post's desire to hire him away from Fortune Magazine.

Justin Gillis

Justin Gillis was paid more than Hamilton on the 1998 salary snapshot and substantially more than Hamilton on the 1999 to 2002 salary snapshots. Gillis was paid slightly more than Mayer on the 1998 salary snapshot and more than Mayer on the 1999 to 2002 salary snapshots. Gillis was paid slightly less than Skrzycki on the 1998 salary snapshot, slightly more than Skrzycki on the 1999 salary snapshot and more than Skrzycki on the 2000 to 2002 salary snapshots.

Experience and Education
Gillis came to The Post in the mid-1990s as a reporter in Metro. He became a reporter in Financial News in 1998 where he remains today. Prior to starting at The Post, Gillis worked at the Miami Herald for approximately 12 years both as a reporter in various departments and most recently as its Urban Affairs Editor. He also served as a news writer for the Associated Press for approximately a year. Gillis is a graduate of the University of Georgia.

Starting Salary
Upon starting at The Post, Gillis received approximately a 20 percent increase over his prior salary at the Miami Herald. His starting salary was more than the salaries of Hamilton and Mayer at that time, but slightly less than the salary of Skrzycki at that time.

Salary History
As of September 1, 2002, Gillis had received five merit increases - all of which he received as a reporter in Financial News. He received merit increases in the following years: 1998, 1999 and 2000.

Explanation:

Starting Salary
The Post cannot locate information about Segal's salary at the Washington Monthly. His starting salary was substantially less than the salaries of Hamilton and Mayer at that time.

Salary History
As of September 1, 2002, Segal had received eight merit increases - two of which he received as a reporter in Financial News. He received those two merit increases in 1999.

Timothy Smart

Timothy Smart was paid substantially more than Hamilton on the 1998 and 1999 salary snapshots.

Smart was paid more than Mayer on the 1998 and 1999 salary snapshots.

Experience and Education
Smart came to The Post in the late 1990s as a reporter in Financial News. He left The Post in 1999. Prior to starting at The Post, Smart worked for over ten years as the Bureau Manager for Business Week. He also was the Associate Editor at Inc. Magazine for six months, a business writer at the Miami Herald for a little over three years, a senior business writer at The Orlando Sentinel for a bit less than two years, and a reporter at the St. Petersburg Times for approximately two years. Smart is a graduate of the University of Florida. He also obtained a MBA from the University of Connecticut.

Starting Salary
Upon starting at The Post, Smart received approximately a five percent increase over his prior salary at Business Week. His starting salary was substantially more than the salaries of Hamilton and Mayer at that time.

Salary History
During his time at The Post, Smart received no merit increases.

Explanation:
Smart was paid a high salary by his previous employer - more than the salary of Hamilton at The Post at that time. Therefore, Smart's starting salary at The Post was substantially more than the salary of Hamilton.

Daniel Southerland

documents.subject: numbered provisions 9-13 of the Post/Guild agreed arbitration procedures governing Title VII compensation discrimination claims
documents.date: approx. 1998-2002 (references September 1, 1994 back-pay cutoff; undated page)
documents.notes: Page 6 of a multi-page arbitration procedures agreement; image rotated 90 degrees. Only this page appears in the batch; not contiguous with the salary report DOC-001 or the other items.

pages.transcript:
[Rotated 90 degrees sideways]

9. The arbitrator's determination shall be limited to a determination of whether the Post engaged in discrimination on the basis of gender, race and/or Hispanic origin in compensation under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. In the event of a finding of discrimination, the arbitrator may award back pay dating to the date of the discrimination, but no earlier than September 1, 1994, and may order prospective adjustment in compensation. No other relief may be awarded.

10. The Post and the claimant (or the Guild when it represents the claimant) shall bear their own costs and attorney's fees. In cases in which the Guild represents the claimant, the Guild and the Post shall split the fees and costs of the arbitrator. In all other cases, the individual claimant and the Post shall split the fees and costs of the arbitrator.

11. In cases in which the Guild does not represent the claimant, it shall be provided with a copy of the claim and decision and, unless the claimant objects, may attend the fact-finding conference.

12. Consistent with the Post's general policy against retaliation and the requirements of law, employees will not be subject to retaliation for participating in a proceeding under these provisions.

13. The time limits established by these Arbitration Procedures may be extended by agreement or upon the approval of the arbitrator.

pages.transcript:
[Rotated 90 degrees sideways]

Post Unit News
Washington/Baltimore Newspaper Guild    No. 21    Date July 13, 1998

GUILD FILES DISCRIMINATION COMPLAINT

Today The Newspaper Guild filed a class action complaint on behalf of our 1,400 members with the D.C. office of Human Rights charging The Washington Post with discrimination on the basis of age, race, national origin and sex.

This action was taken after Guild efforts to persuade management to eliminate discrimination in this shop had failed. The Post has consistently refused to give the Guild definitive information concerning our members, or to discuss the issue of discrimination with us.

It is not an action taken in haste, but after two years without a contract; three years of the Post's refusal to release salary data to the Guild; and a constant refusal on the part of management to even discuss discrimination in compensation at The Post.

Some of the points of the charge:

1. That The Post discriminates on the basis of sex:
- Female reporters at The Post on average earn $121.00 a week less than men - even when their salaries are adjusted for age and tenure.
- Failing to hire and retain qualified women in proportion to their representation in the community. Women are 57% of The Post's work force, yet only one out of five editors or managers is a woman.
- Segregating women in certain lower-paid classifications. 61% of the office and clerical workers employed by The Post are women.

2. That The Post discriminates on the basis of age by:
"...deliberately giving poor evaluations of present and potential performance to older employees by failing to reward older employees commensurately with younger employees; by denying older employees training offered to younger employees by assigning older employees to less desirable positions than younger employees; by promoting younger employees more frequently and to better positions than older employees; and by terminating older employees, and coercing them to leave The Post."

3. That The Post discriminates on the basis of race by:
- Failing to pay blacks and other minorities as much as whites for substantially equivalent work. Black reporters on average earn $31.00 less per week than whites. Other black employees on average make $200.00 less than white employees at The Post.
- Failure to hire blacks, Hispanics and other minorities in proportion to their representation in the community. Hispanics comprise only 1% of The Post workforce, according to the most recent data made available by The Post to The Guild.

(over)

Affiliated with American Federation of Labor-Congress of Industrial Organizations, Canadian Labour Congress.
